paper.title: Live-SWE-agent: Can Software Engineering Agents Self-Evolve on the Fly?
paper.central_claim: Live-SWE-agent is the first live software agent that evolves its own scaffold (custom tools) on the fly during runtime, without offline training, reaching 77.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 45.8% on SWE-Bench Pro and beating manually crafted and offline self-improving agents.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref=null: worker has no access to runtime receipt; model type as configured by controller.

rationale: 运行时由提示驱动的单次任务内工具脚本生成，跨四个LLM在Verified上稳定小幅提升；留存仅限单任务，因果与统计证据偏弱。

materials.notes: Figures 1,3-6 are images (captions only, plus Fig.1 leaderboard values not machine-readable).

evidence.quote: a single run of DGM on SWE-bench costs around $22,000 according to the original paper
evidence.support_explanation: Source for the cost bottleneck of offline self-evolving agents that the paper positions against (DGM figure is quoted from the DGM paper, not re-measured).

evidence.quote: does not make any changes to the agentic loop, impose a particular workflow, or require any costly offline training
evidence.support_explanation: The intervention is confined to prompt text added to an unchanged mini-SWE-agent loop; there is no separate evolution/selection stage.

evidence.quote: we also explicitly ask the agent to reflect on its past trajectory to determine if it should create any tools after each step
evidence.support_explanation: Defines the trigger: a per-step reflection message, not a gap-detector or admission gate.

evidence.quote: we define a custom tool as a script that can be executed in the environment
evidence.support_explanation: The evolved object is a script file in the task sandbox invoked through bash; this is the retained non-weight artifact.

evidence.locator: Sec 4.3 Table 4 (50-problem Verified subset, Claude 4.5 Sonnet)
evidence.quote: Live-SWE-agent w/o tool creation 62.0% 0.00 Live-SWE-agent w/o reflection 64.0% 2.92 Live-SWE-agent 76.0% 3.28
evidence.support_explanation: Only ablation: removing tool creation 62%, tool-creation prompt without reflection 64%, full 76%; single run on 50 problems (12-point gap = 6 problems).
mini-SWE-agent baseline with Claude 4.5 Sonnet on full SWE-bench Verified (500).
Live-SWE-agent with Claude 4.5 Sonnet 75.4% and Gemini 3 Pro 77.4% on Verified; consistent +3 to +5 point gains over mini-SWE-agent across four LLMs; cost increase $0.12 for Claude.

evidence.quote: GPT-5-Mini 53.3% 1231 HGM ( Wang et al., 2025 ) GPT-5-Mini 56.7% 512 Live-SWE-agent GPT-5-Mini 65.0% 0
evidence.support_explanation: Comparison with DGM/HGM on the 60-problem subset; Live-SWE-agent 65.0% with zero offline hours.

evidence.quote: For each baseline, we directly reuse their experimental results and report their performance, cost, as well as the backend LLM used whenever possible
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline numbers (DGM/HGM/SICA, SWE-agent on Pro) are taken from other papers/leaderboards, not re-run under common budget or scaffold.

evidence.quote: GPT-5-Nano fails to understand the goal of creating custom tools and is often stuck in a loop thus leading to reduction in performance
evidence.support_explanation: Counterevidence/boundary: the mechanism hurts weak LLMs (44.0% -> 14.0% on the 50-problem subset).

evidence.quote: SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024b ) Claude 4.5 Sonnet 43.6% - Live-SWE-agent Claude 4.5 Sonnet 45.8% $0.73
evidence.support_explanation: Pro result 45.8% vs 43.6% for SWE-agent (a different, 7,000-LOC scaffold); no mini-SWE-agent control on Pro, so the 2.2-point gap is not attributable to tool creation alone.

evidence.quote: mini-SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024b ) Claude 4.5 Sonnet 40.0% $0.59 Live-SWE-agent Claude 4.5 Sonnet 46.0% $0.66
evidence.support_explanation: Second benchmark/language-family check: +6 points on a 50-problem subset, single run.

evidence.quote: Instead of discarding each evolved agent after a task is completed, we can save and serialize the useful tools and insights
evidence.support_explanation: Authors state that tools are discarded after each task; cross-task persistence is future work. Retention is within-episode only.

evidence.quote: we use a random subset of 50 problems in SWE-bench Verified
evidence.support_explanation: Ablation subset is drawn from the evaluation benchmark itself; no development/test split is described for prompt design.

evidence.quote: Reflect on the previous trajectories and decide if there are any tools you can create to help you with the current task.
evidence.support_explanation: The exact reflection prompt; note it also adds an extra reasoning nudge at every step, which is not separated from tool creation in the ablation.

evidence.quote: maximum step limit of 250 and maximum cost of $3 per issue
evidence.support_explanation: Common step/cost caps inherited from mini-SWE-agent; the cost per issue includes tool-creation overhead.

evidence.quote: does not indicate the result of the edit such that a replacement operation where the string to be replaced does not exist will produce no warning message but still return a success code
evidence.support_explanation: Author-provided concrete reason a self-made tool can help (silent sed failure); anecdotal, no measured frequency.
On the 50-problem subset GPT-5-Mini is 60.0% (mini-SWE-agent) vs 58.0% (Live-SWE-agent), whereas on full Verified Table 1 shows 59.8 -> 63.0: sign differs between subset and full set.

signatures.object: Agent action space (tool inventory) of a bash-only mini-SWE-agent; tools are Python scripts written into the task sandbox
signatures.information: Issue text, repository, full trajectory, each command's return code/output (truncated at 10k chars); no hidden test or gold patch visible; the agent writes its own reproduction scripts
signatures.operation: At each step the agent may emit a bash command or write/modify a script (edit, search, file-analyzer, issue-specific tools) and then invoke it by running the script
signatures.output: Script files in the working environment, reused by later commands in the same trajectory
signatures.conditions: Needs a strong LLM able to decide when a tool is useful (weak LLMs loop); cap 250 steps / $3 per issue
signatures.feedback: Execution output of the commands/tools plus the model's own reading of it
signatures.selection_rule: None: the agent alone decides whether to create, keep or abandon a tool; no admission gate, no held-out check, no version/rollback
signatures.persistence: Files in the sandbox for the duration of one issue; discarded after submission (E013)
signatures.later_use: Later steps in the same trajectory call the script; no cross-task reuse tested
signatures.claimed_effect: Resolve rate +3 to +5 points on full Verified across four LLMs; 62->76 on a 50-problem subset; 45.8% on Pro
signatures.failure_boundary: GPT-5-Nano collapses (44->14), GPT-5-Mini slightly down on the subset; tool count does not correlate with solve rate

signatures.object: The per-step feedback prompt of the agent loop (reflection message appended to every observation) and the initial instruction to create at least an edit tool
signatures.operation: Append 'Reflect on the previous trajectories and decide if there are any tools you can create...' after every command output
signatures.output: A per-step decision point on tool creation (and an extra reasoning nudge)
signatures.conditions: Output shorter than 10k chars (otherwise the warning variant replaces the reflection text)
signatures.persistence: Prompt template (human-authored, fixed across all benchmarks except a path change)
signatures.later_use: Applied at every step of every issue
signatures.claimed_effect: Reflection raises resolve rate 64->76 and tool count 2.92->3.28 on the 50-problem subset
signatures.failure_boundary: Effect confounded with generic extra reflection; no reflection-without-tool-creation control

gap.author_gap: Agents have fixed scaffolds and static action spaces; manual scaffold design is costly; offline self-improving agents (SICA/DGM/HGM) are expensive (~$22k per DGM run) and specialize to benchmark and LLM.
gap.checked_gap: Cost and specialization of offline scaffold evolution is a sourced, concrete bottleneck (DGM cost quoted from original paper, E001; offline hours in Table 2, E008). 'Static action space' as a bottleneck is argued by example (silent sed failures, multi-step grep) rather than measured.
gap.lineage: mini-SWE-agent (bash only) -> SWE-agent (hand-crafted tools, ~7k LOC) -> SICA/DGM/HGM (offline scaffold self-modification on benchmarks) -> Live-SWE-agent (runtime tool synthesis driven by a prompt). Prior tool-creation work for reasoning/embodied tasks is only cited, not compared.
gap.closest_adjacent: DGM/HGM/SICA (same object, offline, benchmark-selected); LATM/CREATOR-style tool-making for non-SWE tasks (named in related work, source text not fixed locally).
gap.residue: Whether runtime-created tools can be kept, validated and reused across issues; whether the gain comes from tool creation or from the added prompt/reflection; behaviour on weaker LLMs.
gap.stakes: Scaffold design cost and the transfer of evolved agents across LLMs/benchmarks.
gap.method_response: Moves evolution to inference time and makes tool creation a per-step decision; avoids offline cost entirely.
gap.remaining_gap: No cross-task retention (E013), no admission/regression gate, no attribution beyond a bundled prompt ablation, weak-LLM failure, leaderboard superiority confounded by differing base LLMs.
gap.unresolved: Nearest neighbours in LLM tool-making literature were not available as fixed local sources; novelty claim 'first live software agent' not independently checked.

rs_pattern.reason: The conventionally fixed component of the iterative agent loop (its tool/action space) is treated as a free design variable and redesigned at inference time; matches the signature identify-fixed-component -> free variable -> redesign for quality/efficiency, though the loop is an agent loop rather than a generative-model sampler.

matches.tactic_steps_checked: Named the fixed component (static action space) with stated reason (hand-designed scaffolds, E001/Sec 1) and ablated removal of tool creation (E005). Not done: separation of the redesign from co-varying prompt content; strongest baseline on same scaffold on Pro; mechanism/theory.
matches.success_checks: Component named: yes. Ablation collapse: partial (62 vs 76, bundled). Order-of-magnitude or incumbent-matching payoff: partial (best open result at time of writing, authors' claim). No retraining/frozen model: yes.
matches.failure_checks: 'Fixed component is bottleneck' asserted by example not measured: partially present. Strong baseline omitted: partly (same-scaffold control absent on Pro).
matches.sub_card_note: C15/C23/C24 are 3D-representation, diffusion-chain and conditioning-interface tactics; none corresponds to tool-set liberation, so sub_id=null.
matches.reason: Operation (not mere mention): the agent's inventory is made mutable during the loop.

matches.condition_checks: H07-step1 gap-detection decision: partial (reflection fires every step). Step2 grounding: unmet (model knowledge only). Step3 sandbox build/repair: partial (agent runs and edits its scripts). Step4 registration/description: unmet. Step5 reuse on tasks that did not produce the tool + retained-inventory ablation: unmet (tools are discarded, E013). S1 execution admission gate: unmet. F1 buried in larger architecture: not present (isolated prompt-only change).

revision_proposals: Consider a sub-condition for within-episode (non-persistent) tool synthesis: H07 assumes registration and later-task reuse.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: RS: free the fixed component of an iterative procedure. Domain: agent forges tools when a capability gap appears mid-task. Both = make the agent's action inventory mutable at runtime.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_or_differences: Domain card additionally requires admission by execution, registration and cross-task reuse; the paper only has in-episode scripts.

expectations.applies_when: A fixed component is claimed to be the bottleneck
expectations.reason: Removing tool creation lowers 76->62 (E005) and the silent-sed / multi-step grep examples (E017) motivate it, but the ablation bundles prompt content and reflection and the bottleneck frequency is not measured.

expectations.applies_when: Always for a method claiming SOTA
expectations.reason: Compared to mini-SWE-agent (same scaffold), SWE-agent (Pro), DGM/HGM/SICA (Verified-60, numbers reused from other papers, E009); no equal-prompt tool-given baseline or other tool-synthesis method.
Same-LLM comparisons exist for mini-SWE-agent (4 LLMs) but the headline 'best of all agents' compares Live-SWE+Gemini 3 Pro to systems with other LLMs (leaderboard figure only).

expectations.applies_when: A tool/skill is admitted to an action space
expectations.reason: No admission step: tools are used immediately, verified only by the agent's own later use.

expectations.applies_when: A tool is claimed to be an abstraction beyond its source instance
expectations.reason: Tools are intentionally issue-specific ('do not need to be general'); no test on inputs the tool was not built for.

expectations.applies_when: Retained library is claimed to carry the gain
expectations.reason: Tool-creation-off ablation exists (E005) but no retained-artifact ablation (e.g., disabling use of created tools, or tool-use frequency/credit).

expectations.applies_when: Forging embedded in a larger architecture
expectations.reason: Failure avoided: the change is an isolated prompt on the unmodified mini-SWE-agent loop (E002), so the forged-tool effect is the measured contribution.
Explicit decision point per step (E003/E015), but forced at every step rather than gated on a detected gap, and weak LLMs loop (E010).

source_refs: BATCH: paper limitations + generic prompt-bundle confound
expectations.applies_when: The method bundles an instruction change with the claimed mechanism
expectations.reason: No control that adds the same reflection/extra-reasoning nudge without tool creation; ablation row 'w/o tool creation' is the base agent (E005, E015).
Single run, no intervals; the same method gives 58 vs 60 (GPT-5-Mini, subset) but 63.0 vs 59.8 on full Verified, showing subset noise (E007, E014, E018).

claims.text: Live-SWE-agent raises SWE-bench Verified resolve rate over mini-SWE-agent for four LLMs (Claude 4.5 Sonnet 70.6->75.4, Gemini 3 Pro 74.2->77.4, GPT-5 65.0->68.4, GPT-5-Mini 59.8->63.0).
claims.setting: 500 problems, one sample per issue, 250 steps/$3 caps
claims.selection_vs_test: No selection stage; prompt development data not described
claims.result_denominator: % resolved of 500; failed runs counted as unresolved
claims.counterevidence: single run; baseline prompt differs in more than tool creation
claims.allowed_conclusion: Prompting for runtime tool scripts is associated with +3 to +5 points on Verified for these four LLMs; cause not separated from added reflection prompt.

claims.text: Both tool creation and the per-step reflection matter (62 -> 64 -> 76).
claims.allowed_conclusion: On this subset the full prompt solved 6 more problems than the tool-creation-without-reflection prompt; direction plausible, magnitude uncertain.

claims.text: 45.8% on SWE-Bench Pro, best known, beating SWE-agent 43.6%.
claims.selection_vs_test: Pro is a separate benchmark, prompt unchanged except path
claims.counterevidence: baseline reused, different scaffold; no mini-SWE-agent control on Pro
claims.allowed_conclusion: Live-SWE-agent scores 2.2 points above the reported SWE-agent figure; not attributable to tool creation alone.

claims.text: Beats DGM/HGM/SICA on Verified-60 (65.0 vs 56.7/53.3/50.0) with zero offline cost.
claims.baseline_control: published numbers of offline self-improving agents
claims.counterevidence: baseline numbers reused; per-issue inference cost of baselines not compared; the same GPT-5-Mini on the 50-problem subset shows 58.0 vs 60.0 for the baseline (E018)
claims.allowed_conclusion: On this 60-problem subset Live-SWE-agent's single-run score exceeds the published scores; cost advantage covers offline cost only.

claims.text: The agent 'autonomously and continuously evolves itself on the fly' (central framing).
claims.counterevidence: tools discarded per task (E013); no gate; weak LLMs degrade (E010)
claims.allowed_conclusion: Within-episode synthesis of helper scripts; cross-task retained self-improvement is not shown.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A prompt that asks a strong LLM to write and reuse helper scripts during one issue is associated with +3 to +5 points of single-run resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified across four LLMs, and +6 on a 50-problem multilingual subset, at modest extra cost.
assessment.cannot_say: That tools are retained or improve later tasks; that tool creation (rather than the added reflection prompt) causes the gain; that it beats offline self-evolving agents under matched LLM/budget; ranking claims versus agents run with other LLMs.
assessment.unresolved: Prompt development split; contamination of Verified for the tested LLMs; tool-usage statistics.
assessment.reproduction_note: All results are author-reported; nothing re-run by us.

G.reason: Concrete, sourced bottleneck (offline evolution cost ~$22k/run, 512-1231 offline hours, benchmark/LLM specialization) and clear lineage SICA/DGM/HGM; remaining gap (no cross-task retention) is stated. Not 4: runtime tool-making literature is only cited, 'static action space is limiting' is argued by anecdote.

M.reason: Mechanism is simple and reconstructible (script tools + per-step reflection) with a plausible reason (silent sed failures, multi-step searches) and a testable prediction (stronger LLMs gain more, weak ones loop). Key assumption that tool creation, not extra reasoning nudges, drives the gain is untested; no selection/retention logic although framed as 'self-evolution'.

X.reason: Operation chain, information visibility, interface (script via bash), caps and exact prompts are fully given (App. D); weak-LLM failure and discard-after-task boundary are explicit. No gate, versioning, rollback, expiry or cross-task read exists, so retention execution is minimal.

E.measurement.reason: Official SWE-bench Verified/Pro/Multilingual hidden-test resolve rates over full benchmark denominators; verifier is standard and not edited by the agent. Reservations: single sample, public benchmarks, headline leaderboard comparisons mix base LLMs.

E.causality.reason: Ablation (62/64/76) and 4-LLM same-scaffold comparison give relevant but bundled evidence: the baseline lacks the whole new prompt, reflection extra reasoning is not controlled, no tool-usage/credit analysis, Pro baseline is a different scaffold, DGM/HGM numbers reused.

E.holdout.reason: Nothing is selected on data (no optimizer), so selection/test leakage is limited to human prompt design, whose data is not described; ablation subset is drawn from Verified; Pro and Multilingual give out-of-benchmark checks with unchanged prompt; contamination of public benchmarks for the LLMs is unaddressed.

E.statistics.reason: Single run everywhere, no intervals or seeds; 50-problem subsets with 12- and 6-point gaps; subset vs full-set inconsistency for GPT-5-Mini. Weak-LLM and failure cases are reported (credit).

E.cost.reason: Average $ per issue reported for Verified, Pro and Multilingual with same caps as baseline, including tool-creation overhead; offline hours of DGM/HGM contrasted. Missing token/step counts, per-issue inference cost of baselines, and cost of failed/aborted runs.
